data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a 'Risk-Minimization Heuristic' that operates purely logically: since falsified theories are known to be false (probability 0) and unfalsified theories are merely not-yet-false, choosing the latter minimizes the certainty of error without asserting the probability of truth.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If all available theories are technically unfalsified but vary wildly in plausibility, making the binary 'falsified/not-falsified' distinction insufficient for action.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'risk' of acting on an unfalsified theory is functionally identical to the risk of acting on a falsified one in specific high-stakes domains.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's own writings explicitly endorse acting on corroborated theories for reasons beyond mere avoidance of known falsehoods.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Logical Elimination of Known Falsehoods. The agent does not predict future success (induction) but avoids known failure (deduction). Preference is defined negatively: it is the refusal to act on a theory known to be false when an alternative exists that is not known to be false.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
